The pop-up draws on these general pools when a people has no verified refugee, migrant or homecoming voice of its own, and for every arrival from a civilization you have not met. The lines come from the displaced of many times and places, and none names who is coming.
Shown on the refugee decision and the Refugees pop-up for a people without a refugee voice of its own, and for every refugee from a civilization you have not yet met.

"Tu proverai sì come sa di sale / lo pane altrui, e come è duro calle / lo scendere e 'l salir per l'altrui scale. (Thou shalt have proof how savoureth of salt / The bread of others, and how hard a road / The going down and up another's stairs.)" — Dante Alighieri, Paradiso XVII (trans. Longfellow)

Dante Alighieri (1265 to 1321) wrote the Divine Comedy in exile, having been banished from Florence in 1302 under sentence of death. In the Paradiso his ancestor Cacciaguida foretells to him how bitter the bread of others will taste.

"Litwo! Ojczyzno moja! ty jesteś jak zdrowie; / Ile cię trzeba cenić, ten tylko się dowie / Kto cię stracił. (Lithuania, my country, thou art like health; how much thou shouldst be prized only he can learn who has lost thee.)" — Adam Mickiewicz, Pan Tadeusz (1834, trans. Noyes)

Adam Mickiewicz (1798 to 1855) is the national poet of Poland. Exiled from the Russian partition, he wrote his epic Pan Tadeusz in Paris after the failed uprising of 1830 to 1831, and never saw his homeland again.
"Thou art like me; for thou resemblest me in wandering and peregrination, and the long separation from relatives and friends." — ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I (attr.), to a palm tree at Córdoba (trans. Gayangos)

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I (731 to 788) was an Umayyad prince who escaped the massacre of his family in Syria, crossed North Africa as a fugitive, and founded the emirate of Córdoba. The verses to a palm tree he planted are traditionally attributed to him.
"Dos patrias tengo yo: Cuba y la noche. / ¿O son una las dos? (I have two homelands: Cuba and the night. Or are the two one?)" — José Martí, Dos patrias, poems of exile (trans.)

José Martí (1853 to 1895) was the poet and apostle of Cuban independence. Deported from Cuba as a teenager, he lived most of his adult life in exile, chiefly in New York, and died in the first weeks of the war he had organised.
"The earth is the mother of all people, and all people should have equal rights upon it." — Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, An Indian's View of Indian Affairs (1879)

Chief Joseph (about 1840 to 1904) led a band of the Nez Perce through a fighting retreat of over a thousand miles in 1877 before surrendering. Exiled with his people to Indian Territory, he argued in Washington and in print for their return.

"Alacres itaque et erecti quocumque res tulerit intrepido gradu properemus (Let us therefore briskly and cheerfully hasten with undaunted steps whithersoever circumstances call us…)" — Seneca, Consolation to Helvia, from exile (trans. Stewart)

Seneca the Younger (about 4 BCE to 65 CE) was a Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman. Banished to Corsica in 41 CE, he wrote his mother a consolation arguing that exile is bearable and that Rome itself is a city of newcomers.
"A free state around me, and a free earth under my feet! What a moment was this to me! A whole year was pressed into a single day." — Frederick Douglass, My Bondage and My Freedom (1855)

Frederick Douglass (about 1818 to 1895) escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the leading African American abolitionist, orator and writer of his century. My Bondage and My Freedom is the second of his three autobiographies.
Shown on the Newcomers pop-up for a people without a migrant voice of its own, and for every newcomer from a civilization you have not yet met.

"exul in Normanniam veni, cunctis ignotus neminem cognovi … inter exteros omnem mansuetudinem et familiaritatem reperi (…arrived in Normandy, an exile, unknown to all and knowing no one. … I found the utmost kindness and attention amongst these foreigners.)" — Orderic Vitalis, Historia ecclesiastica XIII (trans. Forester)

Orderic Vitalis (1075 to about 1142) was born in Shropshire to a Norman father and an English mother and sent at the age of ten to the abbey of Saint-Évroul in Normandy. His Ecclesiastical History is the fullest chronicle of the Norman world.
"So at last I was going to America! Really, really going, at last! The boundaries burst. The arch of heaven soared." — Mary Antin, The Promised Land (1912)

Mary Antin (1881 to 1949) emigrated from Polotsk in the Russian Empire to Boston in 1894 at the age of thirteen. The Promised Land, her memoir of leaving the Pale and becoming American, was a bestseller in 1912.
"…my hopes rose high that somewhere in this teeming hive there would be a place for me." — Jacob A. Riis, The Making of an American (1901)

Jacob Riis (1849 to 1914) emigrated from Denmark to New York in 1870 as a penniless carpenter. He became a police reporter and photographer whose How the Other Half Lives exposed the tenements; The Making of an American is his memoir.

"…my father consented, and gave me his blessing, and my mother took leave of me with tears, while my grandfather laid his hand upon my head…" — Lee Chew, Life Stories of Undistinguished Americans (1906)
Lee Chew left a farming village near Canton for San Francisco in the 1870s and became a laundryman and merchant in New York. His life story was published in The Independent in 1903.
"I should have been here 20 years ago. I just begin to feel like a man." — a migrant writing from Chicago, letter home (1917)

During the Great Migration of 1916 to 1918, hundreds of thousands of African Americans left the rural South for northern cities. Letters they wrote home, collected by Emmett J. Scott, were published in the Journal of Negro History in 1919; the writers' names were withheld.

"Here I am, a youth, a young tree whose roots were plucked from the hills of Lebanon, yet I am deeply rooted here, and I would be fruitful." — Kahlil Gibran, To Young Americans of Syrian Origin (1926)

Kahlil Gibran (1883 to 1931) emigrated from Bsharri in Lebanon to Boston as a boy in 1895. He wrote in Arabic and English, and his book The Prophet is among the most translated works of the twentieth century.

"I left home young and came back old; my accent unchanged, my temples grown thin. The children see me and do not know me; laughing, they ask where the stranger is from." — He Zhizhang, Written on Returning Home (8th c., trans.)

He Zhizhang (659 to 744) was a Tang poet and official who spent nearly fifty years in the capital before retiring to his native Zhejiang. His poem on returning home is among the best known in Chinese.
Shown on the call-home dialog when your own civilization has no homecoming voice of its own.

"There is nothing dearer to a man than his own country and his parents, and however splendid a home he may have in a foreign country, if it be far from father or mother, he does not care about it." — Odysseus, in Homer, Odyssey IX (trans. Butler)

Odysseus is the hero of Homer's Odyssey, who spends ten years after the fall of Troy trying to reach his home on Ithaca. He speaks these words at the court of the Phaeacians, refusing every offer of a better home elsewhere.

"Nescio qua natale solum dulcedine cunctos / ducit et inmemores non sinit esse sui. (By some sweetness I cannot name, one's native soil draws everyone, and will not let them forget it.)" — Ovid, Epistulae ex Ponto I.3, from exile (trans.)

Ovid (43 BCE to 17 CE) was the Roman poet of the Metamorphoses. In 8 CE Augustus banished him to Tomis on the Black Sea, and the Tristia, his poems of sorrow, describe his last night in Rome and his life among strangers.

"I left home young and came back old; my accent unchanged, my temples grown thin. The children see me and do not know me; laughing, they ask where the stranger is from." — He Zhizhang, Written on Returning Home (8th c., trans.)
"Every one who is left far from his source wishes back the time when he was united with it." — Rumi, Masnavi I, proem (13th c., trans. Nicholson)

Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207 to 1273) was a Persian poet and Sufi teacher. Born in Balkh, he was carried west as a child ahead of the Mongol invasions and settled in Konya; the opening of his Masnavi is the reed flute's lament for the reed bed it was cut from.

"con altra voce omai, con altro vello / ritornerò poeta, e in sul fonte / del mio battesmo prenderò 'l cappello (With other voice forthwith, with other fleece / Poet will I return, and at my font / Baptismal will I take the laurel crown.)" — Dante Alighieri, in exile, Paradiso XXV (trans. Longfellow)

Dante Alighieri (1265 to 1321) wrote the Divine Comedy in exile, having been banished from Florence in 1302 under sentence of death. In the Paradiso he imagines returning to be crowned as a poet at the font where he was baptised; he never did.
Abbasid

When people of Abbasid appear in a pop-up, the words are theirs: Abbasid has a voice of its own for the Cultural Enclave decision, the refugee decision and the Refugees pop-up and the Newcomers pop-up. For the call-home dialog the game speaks with the Voices of Many Lands instead. The event fixes the quote, so the same event always shows the same line. Arrivals from a civilization you have not met use the Voices of Many Lands.

When a lasting Abbasid community in one of your cities is recognized as a Cultural Enclave, the recognition pop-up carries one of these lines: the first Abbasid enclave in your empire shows the first quote, the second shows the second. The pop-up appears when enclave recognition is set to Ask me (Options, Add-ons, Emigration, Advanced settings, Cultural enclaves); under the default automatic recognition the city takes the first stance you can afford and the Chronicle records it.

The decision offers two stances drawn from their character, each paid once when you choose it and sized to your own income, or you can simply let them be:[BLIST][LI][B]Fund their learning[/B]: House-of-Wisdom scholars translate, but their stipends drain the treasury (+Science, −Gold).[LI][B]Welcome their envoys[/B]: Their salons and famed gardens receive envoys from across the known world, at the city's expense (+Influence, −Gold).[/LIST]
[B]First enclave.[/B] "Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim." — the Prophet Muhammad, Sunan Ibn Mājah 224

The Prophet Muhammad (about 570 to 632) is the founder of Islam. The saying is a hadith, a report of his words, recorded in the Sunan of Ibn Majah, one of the six canonical collections; it is quoted wherever Islamic learning is praised.
[B]Second enclave.[/B] "We ought not to be ashamed to admire the truth and to acquire it, wherever it comes from…" — al-Kindi, On First Philosophy (9th c., trans.)

Al-Kindi (about 801 to 873) was the first of the Arab philosophers, working in the House of Wisdom at Baghdad under the Abbasid caliphs. His treatise On First Philosophy urges the acceptance of truth from any source.
Shown when refugees from Abbasid reach your gates, on the refugee decision and on the Refugees pop-up that asks where the arrivals should live.
"O neighbour, fate has not dealt fairly between us: come, let me share my sorrows with you, come!" — Abu Firas al-Hamdani, poems from captivity (10th c., trans.)

Abu Firas al-Hamdani (932 to 968) was a Hamdanid prince and Arabic poet of Aleppo. Captured by the Byzantines, he wrote his best-known poems, the Rumiyyat, during years of captivity in Constantinople.
Shown on the Newcomers pop-up when migrants from Abbasid arrive to settle in one of your cities.
"How many a dwelling on earth a young man comes to love, yet his longing is ever for his first home." — Abu Tammam (attr.) (9th c., trans.)

Abu Tammam (about 796 to 845) was an Arabic poet born near Damascus who worked in Egypt before finding patrons at the Abbasid court in Baghdad. He also compiled the Hamasa, an influential anthology of early Arabic verse. The couplet is grouped with his verses by al-Jahiz; other early sources quote it without a name.

[B]First enclave.[/B] "He set up twenty provinces, which they themselves call satrapies." — Herodotus, Histories, Bk. III (trans.)

Herodotus of Halicarnassus (about 484 to 425 BCE) wrote the Histories, the first great work of history in the Greek tradition. He travelled widely and described Egypt, Babylon and Persia as a curious outsider.
[B]Second enclave.[/B] "There are some of these that I planted myself." — Cyrus the Younger, in Xenophon, Oeconomicus 4.24 (trans.)
Cyrus the Younger (died 401 BCE) was an Achaemenid prince and satrap of Lydia. In Xenophon's Oeconomicus he shows a Spartan visitor the garden at Sardis and says he planted some of the trees himself.
Shown when refugees from Achaemenid Persia reach your gates, on the refugee decision and on the Refugees pop-up that asks where the arrivals should live. One of these lines is chosen for each event.

"O Raja of Rajas, give us a place in this city: we are strangers seeking protection who have arrived in thy town and place of residence." — the Zoroastrian refugees, to the Rana of Sanjan, Qissa-i Sanjan (c. 1600, trans. Hodivala)

The Qissa-i Sanjan, a Persian poem of about 1600, is the Parsi community's own account of how Zoroastrians fled Iran after the Arab conquest and were granted refuge on the coast of Gujarat by the local ruler, the Rana of Sanjan.
"Pass by, O heart-kindling breeze of Khorasan, over one left behind, a prisoner in the valley of Yumgan." — Nasir Khusraw, Divan, qasida 236 (11th c., trans.)

Nasir Khusraw (1004 to after 1070) was a Persian poet, philosopher and Ismaili missionary. Driven from Balkh for his faith, he spent his last decades in the remote valley of Yumgan in Badakhshan, writing of his exile.
Shown on the Newcomers pop-up when migrants from Achaemenid Persia arrive to settle in one of your cities.

"I wandered far through the farthest corners of the world and spent my days with every kind of people; in every corner I found some joy, from every harvest I gleaned an ear of grain." — Saadi, Bustan, prologue (1257, trans.)

Saadi of Shiraz (about 1210 to about 1291) is one of the most quoted poets of Persian. He left his city as the Mongols advanced and spent some thirty years travelling before returning to write the Bustan and the Gulistan.
Shown on the call-home dialog when you, as Achaemenid Persia, call your displaced people back to the settlement they fled.
"Since I cannot bear the grief of being a stranger in a strange land, I will go to my own city and be my own sovereign." — Hafez, Divan, ghazal 337 (14th c., trans.)
Hafez (about 1325 to 1390) of Shiraz is the most beloved lyric poet of Persian. His Divan of ghazals is still used in Iran for divination and recited from memory.

[B]First enclave.[/B] "Toûto arésē tê chôra: may this please the country." — Aksumite coinage, bronze coin legend (4th c.)

The kingdom of Aksum, in what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, struck its own gold, silver and bronze coins from the third century onward. Their short Greek and Ge'ez legends are among the few Aksumite words to survive in the kingdom's own voice.
[B]Second enclave.[/B] "Let the people be glad." — Emperor Armah, Aksumite coin legend (7th c.)

Armah was a king of Aksum in the early seventh century, remembered in Islamic tradition as the Negus who gave refuge to the first Muslims fleeing Mecca. His coins carry a Ge'ez legend wishing the people gladness.
Shown when refugees from Aksum reach your gates, on the refugee decision and on the Refugees pop-up that asks where the arrivals should live.

"What shall we do? For we have left our country and our birth-place, and our kinsfolk and the people of our city." — the children of the nobles of Israel, departing with Menyelek, Kebra Nagast, ch. 45 (14th c., trans. Budge 1922)

The Kebra Nagast, the Glory of Kings, is the Ethiopian national epic, set down in the fourteenth century. It tells how Menyelek, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, returned to Ethiopia with the firstborn sons of Israel's nobles, who lament the homes they leave.

[B]First enclave.[/B] "After all, the chief business of the American people is business." — Calvin Coolidge, address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors (1925)

Calvin Coolidge (1872 to 1933) was the thirtieth president of the United States. The line comes from his 1925 address to newspaper editors, a speech that goes on to say that Americans idealise far more than wealth.
[B]Second enclave.[/B] "I hear America singing, the varied carols I hear." — Walt Whitman, I Hear America Singing (1860)
Walt Whitman (1819 to 1892) was the poet of Leaves of Grass. I Hear America Singing, added in 1860, is his catalogue of working people, each singing at their trade.
Shown when refugees from America reach your gates, on the refugee decision and on the Refugees pop-up that asks where the arrivals should live.

"…when my feet first touched the Canada shore. I threw myself on the ground, rolled in the sand, seized handfuls of it and kissed them…" — Josiah Henson, The Story of His Own Life, on escaping slavery (1858)

Josiah Henson (1789 to 1883) escaped slavery in Kentucky in 1830 and reached Upper Canada, where he founded a settlement for other fugitives. His autobiography is often said to have inspired Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom.
Shown on the Newcomers pop-up when migrants from America arrive to settle in one of your cities.
"To her this song meant not so much the acquisition of a new home as the loss of all her friends and relatives." — Hamlin Garland, of his mother, A Son of the Middle Border (1917)
Hamlin Garland (1860 to 1940) grew up on a succession of farms as his family moved west across Wisconsin, Iowa and Dakota. A Son of the Middle Border recalls his mother's grief at each uprooting.

[B]First enclave.[/B] "BÀD ù šal-ḫu-u šá NINA.KI eš-šiš ú-še-piš-ma ú-zaq-qir ḫur-šá-niš (I had the inner wall and outer wall of Nineveh built anew and raised them as high as mountains.)" — Sennacherib, wall-slab inscription, Nineveh (RINAP 3/2, Sennacherib 82, trans.)
Sennacherib (reigned 705 to 681 BCE) was king of Assyria. He made Nineveh his capital and rebuilt it with new walls, palaces and canals, recording the work in inscriptions on its wall-slabs.
[B]Second enclave.[/B] "aḫuz nēmeqi Nabû kullat ṭupšarrūti (I learned the wisdom of the god Nabû, all of the scribal arts.)" — Ashurbanipal, Prism F (RINAP 5/1, Ashurbanipal 9, trans.)

Ashurbanipal (reigned 669 to about 631 BCE) was the last great king of Assyria. He boasted of his scribal training and assembled at Nineveh the library of cuneiform tablets that preserved much of Mesopotamian literature.
Shown on the Newcomers pop-up when migrants from Assyria arrive to settle in one of your cities.
"In July, 1889, I left Oroomiah with not more than what amounts to five dollars in the United States, and not knowing where I should finally land." — Isaac Adams, of Urmia, Persia by a Persian (1900)

Isaac Adams was an Assyrian Christian from near Urmia, in north-western Iran, who emigrated to the United States in 1889 with almost nothing. He trained as a physician and wrote Persia by a Persian about his homeland and his journey.

[B]First enclave.[/B] "dannum enšam ana lā ḫabālim (That the strong might not oppress the weak.)" — Hammurabi, Laws of Hammurabi, prologue i 37-39 (c. 1750 BCE, trans.)

Hammurabi (reigned about 1792 to 1750 BCE) was the king of Babylon who unified Mesopotamia and had his laws carved on a stele. Its prologue names his purpose: that the strong might not oppress the weak.
[B]Second enclave.[/B] "This land is by far the most fertile in grain which we know." — Herodotus, Histories 1.193.2 (5th c. BCE, trans. Godley)

Herodotus of Halicarnassus (about 484 to 425 BCE) wrote the Histories, the first great work of history in the Greek tradition. He travelled widely and described Egypt, Babylon and Persia as a curious outsider.

"Woe is me, I have been exiled from the city, I can find no rest… I am sitting as if a stranger with head high in a strange city." — Ningal, queen of Ur, mourning her people, Lament for Ur, lines 306-308 (early 2nd millennium BCE, trans.)

Ningal is the goddess of the city of Ur in Sumerian religion. In the Lament for Ur, composed after the city's fall around 2000 BCE, she weeps for her scattered people, a form of city lament that Babylon inherited.

[B]First enclave.[/B] "The plantains cover large areas of land; sometimes a garden (so-called) extends for several miles…" — John Roscoe, The Baganda (1911)
John Roscoe (1861 to 1932) was an English missionary and anthropologist who lived in Buganda for twenty-five years. The Baganda (1911) is his ethnography of the kingdom's customs and economy.
[B]Second enclave.[/B] "Agali awamu ge galuma ennyama. (Teeth set together are the ones that chew the meat; unity gives strength.)" — Ganda proverb, coll. F. Walser, Luganda Proverbs
The Baganda of the Buganda kingdom, on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, have a rich tradition of Luganda proverbs. This one was collected in Ferdinand Walser's anthology Luganda Proverbs.
Shown when refugees from Buganda reach your gates, on the refugee decision and on the Refugees pop-up that asks where the arrivals should live.
"Nikodemo conducted his fugitive fellow-Christians to Entare, who hospitably received them owing to his former friendship with Nikodemo." — Robert P. Ashe, Chronicles of Uganda (1894)

Robert Pickering Ashe (1857 to 1944) was an Anglican missionary in Buganda in the 1880s. His Chronicles of Uganda records the persecution of the first Christian converts and their flight to neighbouring Ankole.
Shown on the Newcomers pop-up when migrants from Buganda arrive to settle in one of your cities.

"I remembered the proverb of our forefathers, which they used to sing, "You who stagger about under your burdens, those who come after you will be filled with amazement."" — Ham Mukasa, Uganda's Katikiro in England (1904, trans. Millar)

Ham Mukasa (about 1868 to 1956) was a Buganda chief and writer. He accompanied the Katikkiro, the kingdom's prime minister, to the coronation of Edward VII in 1902 and published an account of the journey.

William Bradford (1590 to 1657) was an English Separatist who fled to the Netherlands to escape persecution and sailed on the Mayflower in 1620. He governed Plymouth Colony for thirty years and wrote its history.

"I never wish to have a better home than I got at present. Thank God, I am well and hearty, and hope that I shall remain so." — John Stedman, labourer, from Upper Canada, letter home (1832)
John Stedman was a farm labourer from Surrey who emigrated to Upper Canada in 1832 with assistance from his parish. His letter home was printed to encourage others to follow.
"Fair these broad meads – these hoary woods are grand; / But we are exiles from our fathers’ land." — Canadian Boat-Song (anon., 1829)
The Canadian Boat-Song appeared anonymously in Blackwood's Magazine in 1829, presented as a Gaelic song of Highland emigrants rowing on the St Lawrence. Its authorship has never been settled.

Robert Burns (1759 to 1796) is the national poet of Scotland. My Heart's in the Highlands, written in 1789 to an old air, was published in the Scots Musical Museum.

"Oh, to be in England / Now that April's there, / And who wakes in England / Sees, some morning, unaware, / That the lowest boughs and the brush-wood sheaf / Round the elm-tree bole are in tiny leaf" — Robert Browning, Home-Thoughts, from Abroad (1845)
Robert Browning (1812 to 1889) was an English poet who spent fifteen years living in Italy. Home-Thoughts, from Abroad, written there, is his best-known poem of longing for an English spring.

"…more than half of the citizens were overcome with longing and pitiful sorrow for the city and the life of their land…" — Herodotus, on the Phocaeans, Histories I.165 (trans. Godley)

Herodotus of Halicarnassus (about 484 to 425 BCE) wrote the Histories, the first great work of history in the Greek tradition. He tells how the Phocaeans of Ionia abandoned their city to the Persians around 540 BCE, and how more than half of them turned back for love of it.
"It was also my fate to be an exile from my country for twenty years after my command at Amphipolis…" — Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War V.26 (trans. Crawley)

Thucydides (about 460 to about 400 BCE) was an Athenian general and the historian of the Peloponnesian War. Exiled for twenty years after failing to save Amphipolis, he used the time to research both sides of the war.

"…he left Aeolian Cyme and fled, not from riches and substance, but from wretched poverty which Zeus lays upon men, and he settled near Helicon…" — Hesiod, of his father, Works and Days (trans. Evelyn-White)

Hesiod (about 700 BCE) was a Boeotian farmer-poet, author of Works and Days and the Theogony. He tells how his father left Aeolian Cyme in Asia Minor to escape poverty and settled at Ascra near Mount Helicon.

"My dear limbs yearn not to stay in the sacred streets of Cyme, but rather my great heart urges me to go unto another country, small though I am." — Homeric Epigram IV (attr. Homer, trans. Evelyn-White)
The Homeric Epigrams are short poems attached to the ancient Life of Homer and attributed to the poet. This one voices a wandering singer resolving to leave Cyme for another country.

"Presently they could hear the soldiers shouting and passing on the joyful word, "The sea! the sea!"" — Xenophon, of the Ten Thousand sighting the road home, Anabasis IV.7 (trans. Dakyns)

Xenophon (about 430 to 354 BCE) was an Athenian soldier and writer who helped lead ten thousand Greek mercenaries out of Persia after their employer's defeat in 401 BCE. His Anabasis records the moment the army, crossing the mountains, first saw the Black Sea and the way home.

"All hail, soil of Argos, land of my fathers! On this happy day in the tenth year I have come to you. Many hopes have shattered, one only have I seen fulfilled." — the Herald, in Aeschylus, Agamemnon 503-505 (trans. Smyth)

Aeschylus (about 525 to 456 BCE) was the first of the great Athenian tragedians. In his Agamemnon, produced in 458 BCE, a herald returning from the ten-year war at Troy greets the soil of Argos before the king himself arrives.

[B]First enclave.[/B] "Agriculture is the great foundation of all under heaven." — Emperor Wen of Han, edict, Book of Han (2nd c. BCE, trans.)

Emperor Wen (reigned 180 to 157 BCE) was the fifth emperor of the Han dynasty, remembered for frugal rule, light taxes and personal attention to farming. The line opens one of his edicts preserved in the Book of Han.
[B]Second enclave.[/B] "When the granaries are full, the people know propriety." — Guanzi, quoted in Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (trans.)

The Guanzi is a Chinese compendium of political and economic thought attributed to Guan Zhong, minister of the state of Qi in the seventh century BCE. Sima Qian quotes its maxim on granaries and propriety in his Records of the Grand Historian.

"All human hearts alike long for their native soil; would hardship or success make any heart differ?" — Wang Can, Rhapsody on Climbing the Tower (c. 208, trans.)

Wang Can (177 to 217) was a poet of the late Han who fled the fall of Chang'an and lived for years as a refugee in Jingzhou. His Rhapsody on Climbing the Tower is the classic Chinese poem of the exile's longing for home.
"Though truly beautiful, this is not my own land; how could I bear to linger here even a little while?" — Wang Can, Rhapsody on Climbing the Tower (c. 208, trans.)

"Let those who arrive first live in peace and contentment, not pining for their old homes, and the poor will call one another to follow and gladly go." — Chao Cuo, memorial on settling new lands (2nd c. BC, trans.)

Chao Cuo (died 154 BCE) was a statesman of the early Han dynasty. His memorials to the throne argued for settling farmers on the northern frontier and for making the first settlers comfortable enough that others would follow.

"Home! Let me go home! My fields and garden are going to weeds; why not return?" — Tao Yuanming, Return Home (405, trans.)

Tao Yuanming (365 to 427) resigned his last official post after eighty days and went home to farm. His Return Home, written in 405, became the classic Chinese statement of leaving public life for one's own fields.

Liliʻuokalani (1838 to 1917) was the last queen of Hawaiʻi. Deposed in 1893 by a group backed by American forces, she wrote Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen in 1898 to plead her people's case against annexation.
"…they return to their parents, but I was returned into tears; for I have no home, neither father nor mother." — Henry ʻŌpūkahaʻia, Memoirs of Henry Obookiah (1818)

"When the east wind blows, send me your fragrance, plum blossoms; though your master is gone, do not forget the spring." — Sugawara no Michizane, on leaving for exile, Shūi Wakashū (901, trans.)

Sugawara no Michizane (845 to 903) was a scholar and minister of the Heian court. Exiled to Dazaifu in Kyushu in 901 through the intrigues of the Fujiwara, he died there; he was later deified as Tenjin, the patron of learning.

"O'er the wide, wide sea, / Towards its many distant isles, / Rowing I set forth. / This, to all the world proclaim, / O ye boats of fisher-folk!" — Ono no Takamura, on his banishment, Kokin Wakashū (838, trans. MacCauley)

Ono no Takamura (802 to 853) was a Heian scholar and poet banished to the Oki Islands in 838 for refusing to sail on an embassy to China. His poem of departure is in the Kokin Wakashū and the Hundred Poets anthology.

"Once there was a man who, finding life in the capital hard to bear, went east … 'Ever more I long for the places I have passed; how I envy the waves that go back.'" — The Tales of Ise, section 7 (10th c., trans.)

The Tales of Ise is a tenth-century Japanese collection of poems set in short prose episodes, following a nameless courtier usually identified with Ariwara no Narihira. Several episodes follow his journey away from the capital to the east.
"Resolved not to stay in the capital, he set off toward the East to find a place where he might live." — The Tales of Ise, section 9 (10th c., trans.)

"Katsura River, sprung from the laurel in the moon: even the reflection in your depths is just as it was." — Ki no Tsurayuki, on the last night of the voyage home, Tosa Diary (935, trans.)
Ki no Tsurayuki (about 872 to 945) was a Heian poet and the chief compiler of the Kokin Wakashū. His Tosa Diary records the sea voyage home to the capital after his term as governor of Tosa.

"When I look abroad o'er the wide-stretched Plain of Heaven, is the moon the same that on Mount Mikasa rose, in the land of Kasuga?" — Abe no Nakamaro, in China, before the voyage home, Kokin Wakashū 406 (trans. MacCauley)

Guðmundur Stefánsson was an Icelandic farmer who emigrated to Wisconsin in 1873 with his family, among the first Icelanders to settle in North America. His letters home describe the departure and the welcome. His son became the poet Stephan G. Stephansson.

Kauṭilya, also called Chanakya, is the author to whom the Arthaśāstra, the Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, is traditionally ascribed. Tradition makes him the minister who raised Chandragupta Maurya to the throne; the received text dates from later centuries.

The Charter Oath was proclaimed in the name of the Meiji Emperor in April 1868, at the start of the Meiji Restoration. Its five articles set the course of Japan's modernisation, the last promising to seek knowledge throughout the world.

"As though driven out with stones, I left my home village, and that sorrow never fades." — Ishikawa Takuboku, A Handful of Sand (1910, trans.)

Ishikawa Takuboku (1886 to 1912) was a Japanese poet who left his village in Iwate for Hokkaido and then Tokyo, living in poverty. A Handful of Sand, his collection of three-line tanka, made him famous shortly before he died of tuberculosis at twenty-six.

"Yokohama deru tok'ya / Namida de deta ga / Ima ja ko mo aru / Mago mo aru (When I left Yokohama, I left in tears; but now I have children, and grandchildren too.)" — holehole bushi, a Hawaii plantation song (Meiji-era emigrants, trans.)

Zheng He (1371 to 1433) was the Ming admiral who led seven great treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean. Before his last voyage he set up a stele at Changle recording how far the fleets had sailed.
[B]Second enclave.[/B] "Knowledge is the beginning of practice; doing is the completion of knowing." — Wang Yangming, Instructions for Practical Living (1518, trans. Henke)
Wang Yangming (1472 to 1529) was a Ming philosopher, general and official. His teaching of the unity of knowledge and action shaped Neo-Confucian thought in China, Korea and Japan.

"My brothers are all scattered; there is no home where I might ask if they live or die. Letters sent never arrive, and still the fighting has not ceased." — Du Fu, Thinking of My Brothers on a Moonlit Night (8th c., trans.)

Du Fu (712 to 770) is, with Li Bai, the most revered poet of the Tang dynasty. The An Lushan rebellion of 755 uprooted him and his family for the rest of his life, and displacement and separation run through his poems.

Yuan Kai was a poet and official of the early Ming dynasty from Songjiang, near modern Shanghai, who served in the capital at Nanjing in the 1370s. He is remembered for a single much-anthologised poem on a letter from home.

Wang Wei (699 to 759) was a Tang poet, painter and official, celebrated for short landscape poems. In this one a traveller from his home town is asked only whether the plum by the window has flowered.
"From tonight the dew turns white; the moon is brighter over my home." — Du Fu, Thinking of My Brothers on a Moonlit Night (759, trans.)
"I lift my head and gaze at the bright moon; I lower my head and think of home." — Li Bai, Quiet Night Thought (8th c., trans.)
Li Bai (701 to 762) is, with Du Fu, the most celebrated poet of the Tang dynasty, and travelled for most of his life. Quiet Night Thought is the poem every Chinese schoolchild learns first.

Henry Marie Brackenridge (1786 to 1871) was an American lawyer and writer who visited the great mounds at Cahokia in 1811 and was among the first to describe them in print.

"Amid the gloom and horrors of the present separation, we are cheered with a hope that ere long we shall reach our destined land…" — George W. Harkins, Choctaw chief, Farewell Letter to the American People (1832)

George W. Harkins (1810 to 1890) was a district chief of the Choctaw. His Farewell Letter to the American People, published in 1832 as the Choctaw were removed west of the Mississippi, is one of the earliest protests against Indian removal in the removed people's own words.

Aeneas is the Trojan hero of Virgil's Aeneid (19 BCE), the founding epic of Rome. He escapes the sack of Troy carrying his father and leads the survivors across the sea in search of a new home in Italy.

Seneca the Younger (about 4 BCE to 65 CE) was a Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman. Banished to Corsica in 41 CE, he wrote his mother a consolation arguing that exile is bearable and that Rome itself is a city of newcomers.

Tecumseh (1768 to 1813) was a Shawnee leader who built a confederacy of nations to resist the sale of their lands. His speeches survive only in the reports of others; he was killed at the Battle of the Thames in 1813.

[B]Second enclave.[/B] "Our lives are in the hands of the Great Spirit. We are determined to defend our lands, and if it be his will, we wish to leave our bones upon them." — Tecumseh, speech to Procter (1813), in Drake (1841)

"We have good homes here, and had abundance of labor and pains to make them. We wanted good men to value our improvements, for we are not ashamed of our homes." — Wayweleapy, Shawnee speaker, council at Wapakoneta (1832)

Wayweleapy was the principal speaker for the Shawnee chiefs of Wapakoneta, Ohio, at the council of 1832 at which the United States pressed them to remove west of the Mississippi. His words were recorded by the council's clerks.
"We pity them, as they are our brethren; we fear that their situation will be ours, when we get ready to start on our journey." — Wayweleapy, Shawnee speaker, council at Wapakoneta (1832)

Mom Rajothai (1819 to 1867) was a Siamese nobleman who served as interpreter to the embassy King Mongkut sent to Queen Victoria in 1857. His Nirat London is the first Thai travel poem about Europe.
"It is only because I am bound to the king's service that I am far from my beloved, far from Siam." — Mom Rajothai, Nirat London (1857, trans.)

[B]First enclave.[/B] "sono molte botteghe di artigiani e mercatanti, e massimamente di tessitori di tele di bambagio (There are many shops of craftsmen and merchants, above all weavers of cotton cloth.)" — Leo Africanus, Description of Africa (1550, trans.)

Leo Africanus (about 1494 to about 1554), born al-Hasan al-Wazzan in Granada and raised in Fez, travelled to Timbuktu and across the Sahara as a young diplomat. Captured by pirates and baptised in Rome, he wrote his Description of Africa in Italian.

[B]Second enclave.[/B] "Vendonsi molti libri scritti a mano, che vengono di Barberia; e di questi si fa più guadagno che del rimanente delle mercatanzie (Many handwritten books are sold, brought from Barbary; and more profit is made on these than on all other goods.)" — Leo Africanus, Description of Africa (1550, trans.)

"O thou who goest to Gao, turn aside from thy path to breathe my name in Timbuctoo. Bear thither the greeting of an exile who sighs for the soil on which his friends and family reside." — Ahmad Baba al-Timbukti, verses from exile in Marrakesh (trans.)

Ahmad Baba (1556 to 1627) was the most celebrated scholar of Timbuktu. After the Moroccan conquest of Songhai in 1591 he was deported in chains to Marrakesh, where he wrote of his longing for home; he was allowed to return only in 1608.

[B]First enclave.[/B] "el que lee mucho y anda mucho, vee mucho y sabe mucho (He who reads much and travels much sees and knows a great deal.)" — Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote II.25 (1615, trans. Ormsby)
Miguel de Cervantes (1547 to 1616) wrote Don Quixote, the first modern novel. He had himself been a soldier, a captive in Algiers for five years, and a tax collector before he wrote it.

[B]Second enclave.[/B] "Nada te turbe; / nada te espante; / todo se pasa… (Let nothing disturb thee, / Nothing affright thee; / All things are passing…)" — Teresa of Ávila, Nada te turbe (16th c., trans. Longfellow)

Shown when refugees from Spain reach your gates, on the refugee decision and on the Refugees pop-up that asks where the arrivals should live.

"Doquiera que estamos lloramos por España, que, en fin, nacimos en ella y es nuestra patria natural (Wherever we are we weep for Spain; for after all we were born there and it is our natural fatherland.)" — Ricote the Morisco, in Cervantes, Don Quixote II.54 (1615, trans. Ormsby)

Ricote is a Morisco villager in the second part of Don Quixote (1615), expelled from Spain with the rest of his people between 1609 and 1614. Cervantes has him return in disguise and speak of his longing for the country that cast him out.
Shown on the Newcomers pop-up when migrants from Spain arrive to settle in one of your cities. One of these lines is chosen for each event.

Rosalía de Castro (1837 to 1885) was the poet of Galicia, writing in Galician at a time when its people were emigrating in huge numbers to Cuba and Argentina. Her Cantares gallegos gave the emigrants their farewell song.

"Adios rios, adios fontes, / Adios regatos pequenos, / Adios vista dos meus ollos / Non sei cando nos veremos. (Farewell, rivers; farewell, springs; farewell, little streams; farewell, sight of my eyes: I do not know when we shall meet again.)" — Rosalía de Castro, Cantares gallegos (1863, trans.)
